coverage_map: social media as a news source

headwords.definition: new information about important or recent events
examples: I usually check the news after breakfast rather than throughout the day.
The local news explained why several roads would close that evening.

headwords.definition: political, social, and economic events being discussed now
examples: Our teacher uses a weekly podcast to introduce current affairs.
Understanding current affairs helps voters evaluate public decisions.

headwords.definition: the title of a news report, designed to summarize or attract attention
examples: The headline sounded alarming, but the article described a small change.
I read beyond the headline before sharing the story.

headwords.definition: a short official news program or announcement
examples: The radio interrupted its music program for an emergency bulletin.
A five-minute bulletin gives commuters the main events without much analysis.

headwords.definition: the latest information about a developing situation
examples: The transport agency posted an update after the storm damaged the railway.
I turned off automatic updates because they were distracting me during class.

headwords.definition: to give someone the newest information or make information current
examples: The reporter updated the article when officials released corrected figures.
Please update me if the meeting time changes.

headwords.definition: information about an important event that is still developing
examples: The channel treated a celebrity argument as breaking news, which seemed excessive.
During genuine breaking news, early details may be incomplete.

headwords.definition: the continuous process through which news is reported and replaced by newer stories
examples: The scandal dominated the news cycle for two days and then disappeared.
A fast news cycle leaves little time to explain complicated policies.

headwords.definition: a person who pays for or regularly signs up to receive media content
examples: Digital subscribers can read the newspaper without advertising.
The newsletter gained subscribers by explaining one issue clearly each morning.

headwords.definition: an arrangement to receive content regularly, often by paying
examples: My library provides a subscription to several major newspapers.
I canceled the subscription because I rarely used the app.

headwords.definition: an organization that publishes or broadcasts news
examples: Several news outlets sent reporters to the flooded region.
A small local outlet may understand the community better than a national channel.

headwords.definition: an important event happening now or recently
examples: Students chose one current event and compared how three sources covered it.
A current event can become easier to understand when its history is explained.

phrases.text: I usually catch up on the news once or twice a day.
The story is still developing, so the details may change.
I try to read beyond the headline.
Local reporting affects my daily decisions more directly.
A short bulletin gives me the main facts.
I don't want constant alerts interrupting my attention.
The issue remained in the news for several weeks.
I heard about the event through a trusted outlet.
The report provided useful background rather than another quick update.
I follow current affairs because public decisions affect ordinary life.
Early reports should be treated with caution.
A subscription can support reporting that takes time and expertise.

headwords.definition: a person who investigates, writes, or broadcasts news
examples: The journalist interviewed residents before describing the housing dispute.
A responsible journalist corrects a factual error openly.

headwords.definition: a journalist who gathers information and reports from events or locations
examples: A reporter at the courthouse explained the decision in plain language.
The sports reporter spoke with both teams after the match.

headwords.definition: a person who selects, checks, and improves material before publication
examples: The editor asked for stronger evidence before approving the article.
A local editor decided that the school closure deserved front-page attention.

headwords.definition: a journalist who reports regularly from a particular place or subject area
examples: The foreign correspondent described how the election affected rural communities.
A science correspondent translated a technical study for general listeners.

headwords.definition: a person, document, or organization that provides information
examples: The article named the public report as its main source.
One anonymous source is not enough to confirm a serious accusation.

headwords.definition: to ask someone questions in order to gather information for a report
examples: The journalist interviewed shop owners affected by the new road.
Before publishing, she interviewed an expert who disagreed with her first source.

headwords.definition: to examine an issue carefully in order to discover facts
examples: Reporters investigated why public funds had not reached the clinic.
The newspaper spent months investigating unsafe conditions at the factory.

headwords.definition: to check that information is accurate or genuine
examples: Editors verified the photograph's date before using it.
I could not verify the claim on any official website.

headwords.definition: to make written or recorded material available to the public
examples: The magazine published a correction beside the online article.
Anyone can publish a video, but that does not make it reliable.

headwords.definition: to transmit a program by television, radio, or online media
examples: The station broadcast the debate live from the university.
Public channels broadcast emergency instructions in several languages.

headwords.definition: the reporting given to an event or subject
examples: Local coverage focused on how the policy would affect bus passengers.
The disaster received extensive coverage while a slower health crisis was ignored.

phrases.text: The reporter spoke to people on both sides of the dispute.
The article draws on public records and firsthand interviews.
Editors need enough time to check important details.
The outlet issued a clear correction.
The investigation revealed a problem that officials had overlooked.
The source requested anonymity for safety reasons.
The report separates confirmed facts from unanswered questions.
Live coverage can show events quickly but without full context.
The journalist translated technical language for a general audience.
Good reporting explains how the information was obtained.
The editor decided the claim needed another independent source.

headwords.definition: consistently accurate and worthy of trust
examples: A reliable source explains where its numbers came from.
I prefer a reliable local newspaper to an unknown account with dramatic posts.

headwords.definition: believable because of strong evidence, expertise, or a trustworthy record
examples: The explanation became more credible when the researchers published their methods.
A professional-looking website is not automatically credible.

headwords.definition: facts or material that support or challenge a claim
examples: The video offered evidence that the road had flooded before the warning.
There is not enough evidence to blame one person for the failure.

headwords.definition: a statement presented as true, although it may still need proof
examples: The health claim spread widely before doctors examined it.
Readers should distinguish the company's claim from an independently tested result.

headwords.definition: to state that something is true, sometimes without proving it
examples: The post claimed that voting hours had changed, but the official notice showed they had not.
A witness claimed to have seen smoke before the alarm sounded.

headwords.definition: obtained directly from personal experience or an original witness
examples: The reporter collected firsthand accounts from passengers on the train.
Firsthand evidence can be valuable, but memory is not always exact.

headwords.definition: an original document, recording, dataset, or witness connected directly to an event
examples: The full court decision is a primary source, while a news summary is not.
Students examined campaign speeches as primary sources.

headwords.definition: background information needed to understand the meaning or importance of something
examples: The chart looked frightening until the article provided ten years of context.
A quotation taken out of context can suggest the opposite of what was meant.

headwords.definition: open about methods, evidence, interests, or mistakes
examples: The outlet was transparent about why it removed the photograph.
Transparent funding information helps readers notice possible conflicts of interest.

headwords.definition: to provide additional evidence that confirms a statement or account
examples: Phone records corroborated the witness's description of the timeline.
Editors waited for a second source to corroborate the allegation.

phrases.text: I would check who produced the information and why.
phrases.reusable_core: who produced the information and why

phrases.text: The article links directly to the original report.
Several independent sources confirmed the same basic facts.
The evidence supports a limited conclusion, not the dramatic headline.
The quotation needs more context.
Expertise matters when the subject is technical.
A trustworthy outlet explains what it still does not know.
phrases.reusable_core: what it still does not know

phrases.text: The author's financial interest should be disclosed.
I could trace the statistic back to a public dataset.
A single personal story cannot prove a general trend.

headwords.definition: false or inaccurate information shared with or without an intention to deceive
examples: Misinformation about the storm caused some residents to avoid a safe shelter.
A relative shared the misinformation because the message looked official.

headwords.definition: false information deliberately created or shared to deceive people
examples: The fake accounts posted disinformation to reduce trust in the election.
Disinformation often mixes real details with a false central story.

headwords.definition: invented or seriously distorted material presented in the style of news
examples: The fake news story copied the design of a familiar newspaper.
Calling every unfavorable report fake news makes useful criticism harder to discuss.

headwords.definition: unconfirmed information passed from person to person
examples: A rumor about school closures circulated before any official announcement.
The company addressed the rumor because employees were becoming anxious.

headwords.definition: a planned deception intended to make people believe something false
examples: The photograph of the unusual animal turned out to be a hoax.
Emergency workers wasted time responding to an online hoax.

headwords.definition: to invent false information, evidence, or a story
examples: The account fabricated quotations and attributed them to a real scientist.
A reporter who fabricates evidence damages trust in the whole outlet.

headwords.definition: likely to create a false impression without necessarily being completely untrue
examples: The graph was misleading because its vertical scale began at ninety percent.
A technically accurate but misleading headline omitted the study's main limitation.

headwords.definition: to investigate whether a public claim is accurate
examples: The organization fact-checked statements made during the debate.
Before sharing the image, I fact-checked its date and location.

headwords.definition: to show with evidence that a belief or claim is false
examples: Medical researchers debunked the popular claim about the vitamin.
The correction arrived too late to debunk the rumor for everyone who saw it.

headwords.definition: to control or alter information unfairly in order to influence people
examples: The video was edited to manipulate viewers' emotional reaction.
A campaign can manipulate statistics by selecting only favorable years.

phrases.text: The post contains a real image with a false description.
phrases.reusable_core: a real image with a false description

phrases.text: I would pause before sharing an emotional claim.
The correction did not reach everyone who saw the rumor.
False information often travels faster than careful verification.
The graph creates a misleading impression by hiding its scale.
The account imitates the appearance of a genuine news outlet.
A fact-check should link to the evidence it uses.
Repeating a false claim can accidentally make it more familiar.
The story combines accurate details with an invented conclusion.

headwords.definition: a preference or tendency that unfairly shapes judgment or presentation
examples: The report showed bias by interviewing only business owners and no workers.
Everyone has some bias, so transparent methods and diverse sources matter.

headwords.definition: influenced by an unfair preference for one side or group
examples: The documentary felt biased because it ignored evidence that challenged its argument.
A source can be biased and still provide some accurate facts.

headwords.definition: not supporting one side in a disagreement
examples: The presenter used neutral language while explaining both proposals.
Complete neutrality may be impossible, but factual standards are still useful.

headwords.definition: including relevant evidence and important perspectives in fair proportion
examples: A balanced report does not need to give equal time to a proven fact and a baseless claim.
The podcast offered a balanced discussion of the policy's costs and benefits.

headwords.definition: to present an issue from a particular angle that influences interpretation
examples: One headline framed the protest as disruption, while another emphasized its demands.
The interviewer framed the question in a way that assumed the policy had failed.

headwords.definition: the particular angle or language used to present information
examples: The framing focused attention on individual behavior rather than government policy.
Comparing the framing across outlets revealed different assumptions.

headwords.definition: a particular way of understanding an event based on experience or position
examples: Local residents offered a perspective missing from the national report.
Reading another perspective does not require accepting every claim it contains.

headwords.definition: an oversimplified and fixed idea about a group of people
examples: The program challenged the stereotype that older adults avoid technology.
Repeated stereotypes can influence hiring even when viewers know a show is fictional.

phrases.text: The choice of words shapes how the audience sees the event.
The report leaves out a perspective that is directly affected.
Balance does not mean treating evidence and speculation as equal.
phrases.reusable_core: treating evidence and speculation as equal

phrases.text: I compare how different outlets frame the same story.
The image encourages sympathy before the facts are explained.
A source can be accurate on one point and biased overall.
The coverage reinforced an old stereotype.
Neutral wording makes the factual question easier to discuss.

headwords.definition: the ability to access, examine, evaluate, and create media thoughtfully
examples: Media literacy helps students notice when an advertisement looks like an ordinary article.
A media-literacy lesson compared the evidence behind three viral claims.

headwords.definition: to judge quality or value using relevant evidence and criteria
examples: Readers should evaluate the source before reacting to a surprising claim.
We evaluated the article by checking its author, evidence, and publication date.

headwords.definition: to compare information with another independent source
examples: I cross-checked the closure notice on the city's official website.
Editors cross-check names and figures before publication.

headwords.definition: to recognize the difference between similar things
examples: Young viewers need to distinguish sponsored content from independent advice.
The article clearly distinguished confirmed facts from the reporter's analysis.

headwords.definition: to decide what information means within its context
examples: Two commentators interpreted the same employment figures differently.
Readers need the full scale to interpret a graph accurately.

headwords.definition: the practice of examining where information originated and whether that origin is trustworthy
examples: Source-checking revealed that the viral quotation came from a parody account.
Simple source-checking can stop a false story before someone shares it.

headwords.definition: paid for by a company or organization as promotion
examples: The influencer marked the phone review as sponsored content.
A sponsored article may contain useful facts, but its commercial purpose should be visible.

headwords.definition: a set of computer rules used to select, rank, or recommend content
examples: The platform's algorithm kept recommending similar political videos.
An algorithm may reward attention without checking whether a story is accurate.

headwords.definition: an information environment where personalized systems repeatedly show similar views
examples: Following only recommended accounts placed him in a filter bubble.
A filter bubble can make a widely disputed belief appear normal and universal.

headwords.definition: a group or space where the same opinions are repeated and rarely challenged
examples: The discussion group became an echo chamber after dissenting members left.
Inside an echo chamber, repetition may be mistaken for independent confirmation.

headwords.definition: the lasting record created by a person's online activity
examples: Sharing an unverified accusation can become part of someone's digital footprint.
Teenagers should know that an old public post may be found years later.

phrases.text: I ask whether the content is informing me or selling something.
The publication date matters when advice can become outdated.
I look for the same fact in an independent source.
The account has a large audience, but that does not prove expertise.
The recommendation system keeps showing me similar viewpoints.
I separate the author's evidence from the author's conclusion.
The label makes the commercial relationship clear.
Media literacy is a daily habit, not a one-time lesson.
I would check the date, author, and original source.
Deleting a post does not always remove every copy.
phrases.reusable_core: does not always remove every copy

phrases.text: The chart may be accurate but easy to misinterpret.
Following thoughtful disagreement can widen an information diet.

headwords.definition: a film or program that presents factual material about real people or events
examples: The documentary followed one farming family through a year of drought.
A powerful documentary can still select scenes to support a viewpoint.

headwords.definition: a digital audio program available as episodes
examples: I listen to a science podcast while walking to campus.
The podcast invited two economists who disagreed about the policy.

headwords.definition: one individual part of a continuing audio or video series
examples: The latest episode explains how local elections are organized.
I downloaded the episode so I could listen without an internet connection.

headwords.definition: the person who presents and guides a program
examples: The host asked short follow-up questions when the guest used technical language.
A familiar host can make a complex topic feel approachable.

headwords.definition: to present a program or provide a place for a public discussion
examples: A local journalist hosts the evening interview program.
The museum hosted an online discussion after the documentary.

headwords.definition: a person whose voice tells or explains a story in recorded media
examples: The narrator connected personal interviews with historical events.
An emotional narrator may influence viewers before the evidence is complete.

headwords.definition: a particular event, especially one that attracts attention or causes concern
examples: The newspaper described the protest as one incident in a longer dispute.
That embarrassing incident received more attention than the policy discussion.

headwords.definition: examining a subject thoroughly and with substantial detail
examples: An in-depth article answered questions that short updates had ignored.
The series offers an in-depth look at how water reaches the city.

headwords.definition: to make an idea or event clear by giving reasons, details, or examples
examples: The animation explained why the bridge moves slightly in strong wind.
Good journalists explain uncertainty instead of hiding it.

headwords.definition: to represent information in a visual form such as a chart, map, or animation
examples: The website visualized changes in rent across different neighborhoods.
A well-designed map can visualize a pattern that is hard to describe in words.

phrases.text: The longer format gives the subject room to develop.
I can listen while doing another simple activity.
The host asks questions a general listener might have.
Personal stories make an abstract issue easier to understand.
phrases.reusable_core: make an abstract issue easier to understand

phrases.text: The documentary has a clear viewpoint rather than complete neutrality.
A visual explanation can reveal the scale of the change.
The episode includes links for further reading.
Long-form reporting can connect an event to its history.
phrases.reusable_core: connect an event to its history

phrases.text: The pace allows listeners time to process unfamiliar ideas.
A convincing story should not replace careful evidence.

sections.title: Social Media, Short Video, and Citizen Reporting

headwords.definition: spreading very quickly among large numbers of online users
examples: A short clip went viral before anyone identified where it was filmed.
Viral popularity reflects attention, not necessarily importance or accuracy.

headwords.definition: a general direction of change or a popular pattern
examples: One dramatic week does not establish a long-term crime trend.
The short-video trend encouraged museums to explain objects in thirty seconds.

headwords.definition: a continuously updated stream of posts selected for a user
examples: My feed contains more international news after I followed several foreign reporters.
Endless scrolling makes it hard to notice how long I have spent in the feed.

headwords.definition: a person whose online audience allows them to affect opinions or purchases
examples: The travel influencer corrected a false claim after local residents responded.
An influencer may have practical experience without professional expertise.

headwords.definition: a person who produces material for digital platforms
examples: The content creator uses simple animations to explain public health research.
Independent creators may cover local interests ignored by larger outlets.

headwords.definition: news gathering or reporting carried out by members of the public rather than professional journalists
examples: Citizen journalism provided early images when professional reporters could not reach the area.
Without verification, citizen journalism can also spread a mistaken account rapidly.

headwords.definition: a person who directly saw an event happen
examples: An eyewitness described the sound but could not see what caused it.
Reporters compared several eyewitness accounts because memory can differ.

headwords.definition: video or audio broadcast online at the same time it is recorded
examples: The council provided a livestream for residents who could not attend.
A livestream showed the crowd continuously rather than through selected clips.

headwords.definition: to broadcast video or audio online as an event happens
examples: A resident livestreamed the flooded street from a safe building.
The organization will livestream the public debate with captions.

headwords.definition: online interaction measured through responses such as comments, shares, or viewing time
examples: The platform rewarded engagement, so emotional posts received greater visibility.
High engagement does not show whether readers understood the article.

headwords.definition: online material with an exaggerated title or image designed mainly to attract clicks
examples: The headline was clickbait because the article never answered its dramatic question.
Repeated clickbait may increase traffic briefly but weaken trust in the publisher.

headwords.definition: to review and manage user content according to rules
examples: The platform hired multilingual teams to moderate comments during the election.
It is difficult to moderate harmful content without removing legitimate criticism.

phrases.text: The clip shows a real event but leaves out what happened beforehand.
Popularity is not the same as reliability.
The platform rewards content that keeps people watching.
An eyewitness can provide valuable detail but may still be mistaken.
Short videos are accessible, but they encourage simplification.
The creator clearly separates sponsorship from personal opinion.
Comments can add local knowledge or spread further confusion.
The full livestream gives viewers more context than one selected moment.
phrases.reusable_core: more context than one selected moment

phrases.text: Content moderation involves difficult judgments about harm and expression.
The title promises more than the report actually delivers.
Citizen reporting is most useful when professional outlets verify it.

sections.title: Public Awareness, Accountability, and Press Freedom

headwords.definition: knowledge and understanding that an issue or situation exists
examples: Local coverage raised awareness of unsafe drinking water.
Awareness alone did not repair the pipes, but it increased pressure for action.

headwords.definition: the requirement to explain decisions and accept responsibility for them
examples: Investigative reporting can strengthen accountability when public money is misused.
Corrections are part of media accountability as well as simple accuracy.

headwords.definition: a person or organization that monitors powerful institutions and exposes wrongdoing
examples: The newspaper acted as a watchdog by examining hidden government contracts.
A watchdog needs legal protection and access to public records.

headwords.definition: the right of journalists and news organizations to report without improper control or punishment
examples: Press freedom allows reporters to investigate leaders without asking their permission.
Legal freedom means little if journalists face violence for ordinary reporting.

headwords.definition: official or private control that suppresses information or expression
examples: The documentary examined censorship during the military government.
Removing a direct threat is different from broad political censorship.

headwords.definition: to remove or prevent publication of material considered unacceptable
examples: Authorities censored photographs that showed the scale of the protest.
The platform was accused of censoring criticism while allowing personal abuse.

headwords.definition: a person who reveals wrongdoing inside an organization
examples: A whistleblower gave investigators documents showing that safety reports were altered.
The law should protect a genuine whistleblower from workplace retaliation.

headwords.definition: the welfare or benefit of society as a whole
examples: Publishing the official's private address was not necessary for the public-interest story.
The editor argued that exposing unsafe medicine was clearly in the public interest.

headwords.definition: the right or ability to keep personal life and information from unwanted attention
examples: The report explained the crime without revealing the child's identity, which protected her privacy.
Public curiosity does not automatically outweigh an ordinary person's privacy.

phrases.text: The investigation brought an ignored problem into public view.
Journalists need protection when reporting on powerful institutions.
The public interest must be weighed against personal privacy.
Access to public records makes official decisions easier to examine.
A free press can expose wrongdoing, but it also needs ethical limits.
The story created pressure for an official response.
The source faced retaliation after revealing the documents.
Censorship can hide a problem without solving it.
The report gave citizens information they needed to participate.

sections.title: Information Overload and the Future of News

headwords.definition: difficulty understanding or deciding because too much information arrives at once
examples: During the emergency, conflicting alerts created information overload.
Information overload can make people avoid the news completely.

headwords.definition: tiredness or avoidance caused by repeated exposure to distressing news
examples: After weeks of war coverage, she experienced news fatigue and limited her updates.
News fatigue does not mean that a person has stopped caring.

headwords.definition: to keep viewing upsetting online news for a long time despite feeling worse
examples: I started to doomscroll after midnight and slept badly.
Turning off alerts makes me less likely to doomscroll during a crisis.

headwords.definition: unable to cope comfortably because there is too much information or pressure
examples: I felt overwhelmed by dozens of contradictory reports after the earthquake.
A daily summary helps readers stay informed without becoming overwhelmed.

headwords.definition: the process of adapting content to an individual user's interests or behavior
examples: News personalization helps me find science stories but may hide unfamiliar issues.
The app allows users to control some of its personalization settings.

headwords.definition: a system that requires payment before online content can be read
examples: The detailed investigation was behind a paywall, but the emergency information remained free.
Paywalls fund reporting while limiting access for people who cannot subscribe.

headwords.definition: a service that collects and organizes reports from many publishers
examples: The news aggregator showed several accounts of the same election result.
An aggregator may send traffic to journalism without producing reports itself.

headwords.definition: images, audio, or video created or substantially altered by artificial intelligence
examples: Synthetic media can produce useful translations as well as convincing deceptions.
The channel labeled the reconstructed voice as synthetic media.

phrases.text: I limit news checks to specific times of day.
A summary can reduce overload without hiding major developments.
Personalization helps with relevance but may narrow exposure.
People need a practical way to identify AI-generated material.
Quality reporting costs money to produce.
Essential emergency information should remain freely accessible.
I would rather receive one useful digest than dozens of alerts.
Constant exposure to distressing stories can lead to avoidance.
